source_text: Ἔδοξα δέ ποτε τὸ μέγιστον τῶν ἀγαθῶν βρῶσιν εἶναι καὶ πόσιν· κἀκεῖνον θεοφιλέστατον, ὃς ἂν τούτων ἀπολαύῃ παρὰ τὸν βίον, ὡς οἷόν τε μάλιστα· καὶ παραμυθίαν τῆς ζωῆς, τὴν τοιαύτην εὐθυμίαν μόνην ἡγησάμην· καὶ τοίνυν προσεῖχον οὐδενὶ ἑτέρῳ, ἢ τῇ οἰήσει ταύτῃ, ὡς μήτε νύκτωρ μήτε μεθημέραν ἁπάντων, ὅσα πρὸς τρυφὴν ἀνθρώποις εὕρηται, ἐμαυτὸν ἀπάγειν. Ἔγνων τε τοσοῦτον, ὅτι ἐν ἐκείνοις τὶς ἐμφύρων, οὐδαμῶς δυνήσεται, οὐδὲ πολλὰ μοχθήσας, εὑρεῖν τὸ ὄντως ἀγαθόν.
thought_title: The mistake of living for food and drink
orientation: Solomon admits he once thought eating and drinking the greatest good, and learned that such a life never finds what is truly good.
pass_a_gloss: I once thought the greatest of goods to be eating and drinking; and that one most God-beloved who enjoys these during life as much as possible; and I considered such cheerfulness the only consolation of life; and so I attended to nothing else than this notion, so as neither by night nor by day to lead myself away from all things that have been found for luxury by men. And I knew this much, that one mixing/soiling himself in those things will in no way be able, not even having toiled much, to find the truly good.

pass_b_english: I once thought that the greatest of goods was eating and drinking, and that the man dearest to God was the one who enjoyed these things in life as much as he possibly could (Ecclesiastes 8:15). I held that such good cheer was the only comfort of life, and so I attended to nothing else but this notion, so that neither by night nor by day did I keep myself away from anything people have discovered for luxury (Ecclesiastes 8:16). And I learned this much: that someone who mires himself in those things will never be able, not even with much toil, to find what is truly good (Ecclesiastes 8:17).
notes: Numbering is the same in English and LXX. Gregory turns the praise of eating and drinking in 8:15 into Solomon's former, mistaken opinion (ἔδοξα ποτε, 'I once thought'); the English keeps the past tense so the view is not read as the author's teaching. 'Neither by night nor by day' follows 8:16 ('neither day nor night does one see sleep'). 'Mires himself in' renders ἐμφύρων, present participle of ἐμφύρω ('mix oneself up in', with a sense of soiling; the 1622 Latin has 'se his rebus inquinaverit') (source row note).
